questions.question: Which example best describes Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

options.text: Using a complete web-based email application.
Renting virtual machines and managing their operating systems and applications.
Buying a physical computer for your home.
Editing a document stored only on your laptop.

questions.explanation: IaaS provides infrastructure such as virtual machines, storage and networking. Customers typically manage the operating systems and applications running on their virtual machines.

questions.question: What is a main benefit of Platform as a Service (PaaS)?

options.text: It removes the need to write or maintain application code.
It guarantees that applications never fail.
It requires customers to maintain the provider's physical servers.
It lets developers deploy applications while the provider manages much of the underlying platform.

questions.explanation: PaaS reduces infrastructure and platform management work. Developers still need to manage their application code, data and relevant configuration.

questions.question: Which example best describes Software as a Service (SaaS)?

options.text: Using a provider-managed online email service through a browser.
Installing an operating system on a rented virtual machine.
Assembling a physical server.
Configuring network cables in a data center.

questions.explanation: SaaS delivers a ready-to-use application over a network. The provider manages the application infrastructure, while customers manage their usage, data and available settings.

questions.question: What is a cloud region?

options.text: A user's password policy.
A folder containing application source code.
A geographic area where a cloud provider operates infrastructure.
A programming language used for cloud applications.

questions.explanation: A region is a geographic location for cloud infrastructure. Region selection can affect latency, service availability and data-location requirements.

questions.question: Why might an application be deployed across multiple availability zones within a region?

options.text: To eliminate the need for backups.
To reduce the impact of a failure affecting one zone.
To make authentication unnecessary.
To guarantee zero operating costs.

questions.explanation: Availability zones provide separate infrastructure locations within a region. An appropriately designed application can continue operating when one zone has a failure.

questions.question: Before sending real user traffic to a newly deployed application, what should you do?

options.text: Remove all application logs.
Make every configuration value public.
Disable authentication to simplify testing.
Verify configuration, required connections and application health.

questions.explanation: Deployment checks help confirm that the application starts correctly, has the required configuration and can reach its dependencies before users rely on it.

questions.question: What does the principle of least privilege mean?

options.text: Grant only the permissions needed to perform a task.
Give every user administrator access.
Use one shared administrator account for everyone.
Allow access without checking identity.

questions.explanation: Least privilege limits access to what a person or service needs. This reduces the potential impact of mistakes or compromised accounts.

questions.question: An application needs a private database password. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Commit it to a public source-code repository.
Include it in JavaScript sent to every user's browser.
Store it in a protected secrets service and grant the backend only the access it needs.
Print it in every application log message.

questions.explanation: Private credentials should be protected and accessible only to authorized services. Browser-delivered code and public repositories cannot keep a database password secret.
